findings.passage: Both types would have hidden the knee. Only one explanation matches what he said.
findings.problem: The Six-over-Three tiebreaker rests on an everyday idiom. In the Empire audio (S28), the host asks "How? What happened?" and Harries tells the injury as a comic anecdote, opening by downplaying it ("people live ... capable lives without ACLs"). "For fear of losing this job" is how anyone of any type would describe hiding an injury from a studio. Losing a career-making lead is as much a loss of status and image as of security. The draft's own evidence record concedes this (type_hypothesis.unexplained: "the career stakes would push any type the same way"). The draft's own causal bridge also undercuts the tiebreaker: "He already saw himself as the risky bet. He was not going to hand anyone a reason to agree" describes protecting how decision-makers see him, which is the Three reading. That sentence is also an imagined motive, extrapolated from an October 2026 retrospective remark to a 2025 decision.
findings.acceptance_test: The Three section no longer claims the ACL motive phrase discriminates Six from Three. It says the stated motive fits both, and the discriminator against Three rests on something else in the record (or the margin is stated as narrow). The "not going to hand anyone a reason to agree" sentence is either removed or labeled as the author's inference, and it acknowledges that the inference also fits Three.

findings.passage: Harries does use escapes, video games and cycling, but he names them as anxiety management, not as fun.
findings.problem: The rebuttal misstates the rival. Seven is a head-triad fear type, and its signature move is distracting from anxiety through stimulation. "I played Elden Ring to switch my brain off during the three months I was screen testing" and "I was out riding my bike trying to distract myself" are textbook Seven avoidance. His calling it anxiety does not count against Seven; Sevens feel the anxiety they are escaping. This is the article's lead argument against its strongest alternative, so the Six case looks stronger than the evidence allows. The remaining anti-Seven points are one quote each (motorbike certainty, 2022; "terrifying," 2026), and in the second he went in blind anyway, by choice, on a film he "loved."
findings.acceptance_test: The Seven section no longer treats naming anxiety as evidence against Seven. The escapes are presented as neutral or Seven-leaning. The remaining discriminator is stated with its limits: single quotes, and he chose to go in unprepared. The text says plainly how narrow the Six margin is.

findings.passage: Hiding a torn knee and doing the stunt anyway is a counterphobic move.
findings.problem: The counterphobic subtype is asserted as fact in the type section, then used to absorb contrary evidence. In the counterevidence section it returns as "That is consistent with a counterphobic Six" for the fights, the jokes, challenging a director and the improvised scene. Cautious preparation counts as Six; bold risk-taking counts as counterphobic Six. That makes the thesis unfalsifiable, which the standard explicitly forbids ("Do not use wings/arrows/subtypes to explain away every contradiction"). Concealment is also not the same as confronting a fear head-on: hiding the injury avoided the feared conversation until a stunt forced it.
findings.acceptance_test: The counterphobic label is hedged as a possibility, not stated as a classification of the ACL decision. Bold or provocative behavior is not counted as Six evidence. The article names at least one observable behavior that would count against the Six reading rather than being absorbed by a subtype.

findings.passage: Fear is what he says powers him, from beating himself up over missed auditions in 2015 to hiding his knee in 2025.
findings.problem: The 'fear is his engine' thesis (also in the title) ignores composure evidence in sources the draft already cites. On release day he told Cultured (S03), "I went through a phase of being nervous ... I’ve gone past the point of nervousness. Now I’m just like, ‘Hey, that’s the film.’" The same writer calls him "clear-eyed and methodical" and says he handles the pressure "with aplomb." Square Mile's 2022 profile (S01) opens, "The first thing you notice about Tom Rhys Harries is how relaxed he is." He offered to hold his breath "for like three minutes" in a sealed mask until insurers refused (S03). The evidence record lists Nine as a fit for this calm surface, but the article never mentions Nine. Meanwhile it counts Nine-compatible lines as Six evidence: "what is meant for you, won’t pass you by," "Do not tell me who else it is" and "nothing is going to change." Fear-talk in S02 is also partly prompted: he says "fear is a mark of caring" in reply to Connor's "I was shit scared, as I think you should be."
findings.acceptance_test: The body quotes or paraphrases the release-day "past the point of nervousness" line and at least one interviewer's observation of his calm, and explains how the fear thesis survives them. Nine gets at least a sentence of honest consideration where the acceptance and tuning-out lines appear. The title and description language about fear is checked against this added counterevidence.

findings.passage: He put the win in the network, and he named loyalty as the only plan.
findings.problem: The ending's "sharpest test" is one post-release press interview. The draft admits that gratitude to the crew is press etiquette, then overrides that caveat. The quote is cut short: in THR (S26) the sentence goes on, "fundamentally nothing is going to change — it might open a few more doors in terms of who I’m able to talk to." "Projects from creators who I back fundamentally" is a taste in collaborators, not a statement that loyalty is "the only plan." The closing line ("It is a very Six thing to say after a win") rests on a statement the evidence record says a Nine could equally make. Calling it the sharpest test also says the article's ending was set up in advance as a settle test, and the reading passes it by interpretation, not by a distinctive behavior.
findings.acceptance_test: The "sharpest test" framing is softened to one interview, consistent with Six but not decisive. The omitted "open a few more doors" clause is included or the paraphrase no longer implies he ruled out change. "Named loyalty as the only plan" is replaced by language that matches what he said. The final paragraph no longer presents the quote as distinctively Six.

findings.passage: Since 2015 he has described fear as what drives his focus and preparation as a crutch
findings.problem: The dates are wrong, and this sentence is in both the 60-word type answer and the type FAQ. The 2015 WhatsOnStage piece (S04) shows only that he beat himself up over missed auditions. It says nothing about fear driving focus. The earliest fear-as-driver statement found is Square Mile in 2022 (S01), and "crutch" comes from Interview in September 2026 (S02). The body itself says the fear language appears "In 2022."
findings.acceptance_test: The type answer and the FAQ answer date each claim to its source (fear as driver: 2022; preparation as a crutch: 2026), or use "in interviews since 2022." No sentence implies that a 2015 source shows fear as his engine.

findings.passage: Asked why he hid an injury that could have ended the job anyway, the reason he gave was fear.
findings.problem: He was not asked why. In the Empire audio the host asks "How? What happened?" and Harries volunteers the motive mid-story, in a light, joking register. "Could have ended the job anyway" is the author's inference, not something anyone in the record says.
findings.acceptance_test: The sentence describes the motive as volunteered while telling the story, notes the comic register or drops the 'asked why' framing, and either drops "could have ended the job anyway" or marks it as inference.

findings.passage: Harries told [Square Mile](https://squaremile.com/culture/film-tv/tom-rhys-harries-interview/) that he lives with ADHD
findings.problem: This attributes a health disclosure as direct speech when the source has it in the writer's voice. "He lives with ADHD, a condition that was occasionally tricky in his school days" is Michael Rudling's narration. Harries's quoted words in the piece ("I don’t know any different ... I’m shit at focusing on something if I’m not interested in it") never name the condition. The FAQ goes further: "He has said so himself." Medical claims call for careful attribution.
findings.acceptance_test: The body and the ADHD FAQ attribute the ADHD statement to Square Mile's reporting of the interview (e.g. "Square Mile reported in 2022 that he lives with ADHD; in the same interview he said ..."). Neither says he stated it in his own words unless a source with his own words is opened.

findings.passage: sits in the head triad, the three types organized around fear. What separates them is the response.
findings.problem: The similarity diagnostic tripped (score 1.0) on this clause: "the three types organized around fear" appears verbatim in the recent Paul Bettany profile. The next sentences in the primer, "Some Sixes go straight at the thing that scares them," closely paraphrase Bettany's "Some charge straight at the threat" (0.122). The whole paragraph is a reusable type primer, not Harries-specific, and its counterphobic sentence feeds critic-03.
findings.acceptance_test: No sentence is shared verbatim with the Bettany page. The primer paragraph is either shortened to what a new reader needs or anchored in a Harries detail, and the similarity check no longer trips on it.

protected_passages.passage: His later podcast account and Watkins's agree that the secret came out mid-shoot instead.
protected_passages.reason: Honestly reconciles the overstated EW relay with the unscripted audio and the director's account instead of using the more dramatic version.

protected_passages.passage: The ADHD disclosure cuts against both readings. It explains the breadth of interests without needing Seven, and it explains the hyperfocus without needing Six.
protected_passages.reason: A real confound handled fairly: the article removes evidence from both sides instead of only from the rival.

protected_passages.passage: That is premiere-season praise from a castmate, published by a site that gets his age wrong, so it carries limited weight.
protected_passages.reason: Grades its own testimony in the reader's view; a model for how weak sources should be handled.

protected_passages.passage: A Seven wants more doors open. This is a man who relaxes when a question has one right answer.
protected_passages.reason: Memorable, specific and tied to a verified 2022 quote; the best line in the rival-type section (keep it even if the surrounding argument is narrowed).

protected_passages.passage: This is his account of his childhood, not a diagnosis of it, and it does not explain his type.
protected_passages.reason: Refuses the childhood-wound causal story the standard warns against while keeping the vivid detail.

assessment: A well-sourced, unusually honest draft with a hook it earns: the ACL story is pinned in unscripted audio and corroborated by the director, and weak sources are graded in the reader's view. The skeptical problem is the type verdict. Its two decisive moves, "only one explanation matches what he said" against Three and "anxiety management, not fun" against Seven, fail on inspection. The first rests on an everyday idiom the evidence file concedes any type would use. The second misdescribes Seven, whose distraction is itself anxiety avoidance. The counterphobic subtype then absorbs every bold or provocative act, so the Six case cannot lose. The draft also leaves out composure evidence from sources it already cites ("past the point of nervousness," "how relaxed he is," "clear-eyed and methodical"), never mentions the Nine alternative its own research raised, and builds its ending on a truncated, Nine-compatible quote. One dating error ("Since 2015") sits in the type answer and the FAQ. Six may still be the best read, but at medium confidence the argument should say how narrow the margin is. Contested typing stays flagged; no new risk categories.
